title: Blue Box recycling advocacy and police CCTV plans
subtitle: Reep Green Solutions update, a Hazel Street apartment proposal, and reconciliation and refugee housing remarks.
overview: Council's only substantive decision was to ask the province to change Ontario's Blue Box regulation. Under the current rules, producers are not responsible for recycling from sources such as places of worship, shelters, food banks and public areas of municipal buildings. If the City keeps serving them, it would carry the full cost. Council passed the request {{vote:m1}} and will send it to provincial ministers, local MPPs, municipal associations and other municipalities.

Council also heard from Waterloo Regional Police Service about a planned camera program using CCTV and licence plate readers. Councillors raised concerns about equity, bias, cost and public engagement. The presentation was for information only, and no vote was taken. Police said a public information evening is set for November 12 and that the privacy impact assessment is still being finalized.

In an informal public meeting, staff and an applicant outlined a proposed six-storey, 40-unit building at 277 and 279 Hazel Street in Northdale, with four parking spaces. No decision was made, and staff will report back later. Council also heard an update from Reep Green Solutions and marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

decisions.detail: Council asked the province to amend the Blue Box regulation so producers are responsible for recycling from all sources, including places of worship, shelters, food banks and municipal buildings, and asked other Ontario municipalities for support {{vote:m1}}.

debate: On CCTV, councillors asked whether camera locations could lead to disproportionate surveillance of racialized and low-income neighbourhoods. Police said locations were chosen using crime data and calls for service, and that engagement would include the police equity, diversity and inclusion unit.

One councillor cited research suggesting video systems can misidentify some groups and may be less effective against violent crime. Police said search categories such as race are prohibited, a person must review every result, and the cameras have no facial recognition. Police acknowledged more long-term research is needed.

Councillors asked about cost and what happens if the provincial grant ends. Police said the first phase costs just under $200,000, with half covered by the grant, and that future costs would be planned through budgets. One councillor asked about balancing this with community-based prevention, and police said the two must go together.

On the Hazel Street proposal, councillors asked about parkland, reduced setbacks, usable landscaped space, and only four parking spaces. Staff said transportation staff had no parking concerns because the site is in a major transit station area. The applicant's representative said fewer parking spaces support affordability.

Councillors urged more two- and three-bedroom units, and the applicant's representative said that would be considered. Asked about affordability, the representative said the building is intended as purpose-built rental, likely for students, and may not meet the definition of affordable.
